entry.title: Debate 304: Richard Swinburne vs Bart Ehrman — God and Suffering · 2009
entry.summary: Ehrman’s victim-centered, natural-evil, and scriptural challenges outweighed Swinburne’s coherent but incompletely warranted account of responsible freedom, sanctity, redemption, and heaven.

entry.title: Debate 303: William Lane Craig vs Michael Nugent — Does God Exist? · 2017
entry.summary: A close contest in which Nugent’s method and targeted rebuttals narrowly outperformed Craig’s structured cumulative case, while both left central grounding questions unresolved.

entry.title: Debate 302: Randal Rauser vs Dan Barker — Is the Christian God Worthy of Worship? · 2020
entry.summary: Rauser narrowly prevailed by making his Christian framework explicit and conditional, while Barker's victim-centered objections kept the central moral burden unresolved.

entry.title: Debate 301: David Wood vs Shabir Ally — Did Jesus Rise from the Dead? · 2018
entry.summary: Wood’s cumulative historical case leads, while Ally’s critical challenges expose narrative tensions without establishing his conditional survival-and-ascension alternative.

entry.title: Debate 300: Daniel Dennett vs Robert Sapolsky — Do We Have Free Will? · 2023
entry.summary: Sapolsky narrowly prevailed by pressing unchosen causal origins, while Dennett built a strong compatibilist account of evolved, reasons-responsive self-control and humane responsibility.

entry.title: Debate 299: Paulogia vs Michael Jones — Divine Hiddenness and a Perfectly Loving God · 2019
entry.summary: Paulogia narrowly wins through the one-exception burden and unequal disclosure, while Jones offers calibrated psychological, public-evidence, and postmortem compatibility replies.

entry.title: Debate 298: Trent Horn vs Raphael Lataster — Does God Exist? · 2016
entry.summary: Horn offers four converging routes to classical theism; Lataster narrowly prevails by preserving premise uncertainty, probabilistic counterevidence, and unresolved supernatural rivals.

entry.title: Debate 297: Mike Winger vs Paulogia — Evidence for the Resurrection · 2018
entry.summary: Mike Winger and Paulogia dispute whether early resurrection reports, appearances, persecution, and the empty tomb make Jesus’s resurrection the best historical explanation.

entry.title: Debate 296: Matt Dillahunty vs Randal Rauser — Humanism or Christianity? · 2023
entry.summary: Matt Dillahunty and Randal Rauser compare secular humanism and mere Christianity as practical foundations for equal worth, moral judgment, solidarity, and present human flourishing.

entry.title: Debate 295: Trent Horn vs Paulogia — Did the Apostles Die for a Lie? · 2023
entry.summary: Horn argues that documented and foreseeable suffering supports apostolic sincerity; Paulogia answers that evidence for several named leaders cannot establish all eleven.

entry.title: Debate 294: Paul Copan vs Randal Rauser — The Canaanite Conquest and a God of Love · 2022
entry.summary: Copan defends a historically grounded, hyperbolic conquest under exceptional divine judgment; Rauser argues that residual civilian targeting and identity destruction remain morally indefensible.

entry.title: Debate 293: Sean McDowell vs Paulogia — Apostolic Martyrdom and the Resurrection · 2020
entry.summary: McDowell argues costly apostolic persistence supports sincere resurrection belief, while Paulogia accepts key individuals but challenges group scope, death evidence, and the move from sincerity to truth.

entry.title: Debate 292: SJ Thomason vs Scott Clifton — Morality, Meaning and God · 2020
entry.summary: Clifton’s careful separation of moral facts, duties, and finite meaning outperformed Thomason’s suggestive but under-supported appeals to transcendence and higher calling.

entry.title: Debate 291: Randal Rauser vs Justin Schieber — Does God Exist? · 2015
entry.summary: Schieber’s comparative naturalist case better connects simplicity, hiddenness, cosmic hostility, and suffering to the motion, while Rauser offers serious epistemic and moral replies.

entry.title: Debate 290: Randal Rauser vs Alex Malpass — Does Suffering Provide Evidence Against Theism? · 2021
entry.summary: Malpass argues suffering favors indifference over classical theism; Rauser concedes the bare comparison while defending richer theistic background beliefs.

entry.title: Debate 289: Erik Wielenberg vs Adam Lloyd Johnson — What Is the Best Account of Objective Morality? · 2020
entry.summary: Wielenberg’s focused parity, intrinsic-value, and obligation challenges outperformed Johnson’s theistic grounding, though Johnson pressed a serious evolutionary reliability problem.

entry.title: Debate 288: Michael Shermer vs Luuk Vandeweghe — Are the Miracles of Jesus Unbelievable? · 2019
entry.summary: Shermer wins by pressing claim-specific evidence and comparative religious testimony, while Vandeweghe offers substantive but incompletely connected historical witness arguments.

entry.title: Debate 287: Adam Lloyd Johnson vs Dan Barker — Does God Exist? · 2022
entry.summary: Johnson narrowly wins by presenting the more integrated cumulative case, though Barker’s coherence and evidential objections substantially limit its force.

entry.title: Debate 286: Samuel Nesan vs Matt Dillahunty — Did Jesus Fulfill Prophecy? · 2021
entry.summary: Dillahunty’s two-stage demand for prospective specificity and independent event evidence outweighed Nesan’s thoughtful but insufficiently constrained cumulative covenant reading.

entry.title: Debate 285: Kyle Butt vs Dan Barker — Does the God of the Bible Exist? · 2009
entry.summary: Dan Barker narrowly wins through stronger natural alternatives and direct corrections, while Kyle Butt delivers the best single rebuttal on testimony but leaves key biblical identification bridges unsupported.

entry.title: Debate 284: William Lane Craig vs Klemens Kappel — Does God Exist? · 2012
entry.summary: Craig’s cumulative theistic arguments face Kappel’s qualified atheism, comparative naturalism, and challenges concerning explanation, morality, testimony, and disagreement.

entry.title: Debate 283: Dinesh D’Souza vs Dan Barker — Does God Exist? · 2009
entry.summary: Barker narrowly wins by sustaining evidential restraint and sharper rebuttals, while D’Souza offers a broad cumulative case weakened by several unsupported inferential bridges.

entry.title: Debate 282: William Lane Craig vs Andrew Pyle — Does the Christian God Exist? · 2007
entry.summary: Pyle’s burden-sensitive critiques expose decisive identification and probability gaps, while Craig presents a clear cumulative case whose resurrection bridge remains contested.

entry.title: Debate 281: Blake Giunta vs Matt Dillahunty — Did Jesus Rise from the Dead? · 2016
entry.summary: Dillahunty wins by separating early proclamation from resurrection, while Giunta offers substantial historical and Bayesian replies that leave important evidential bridges unresolved.

entry.title: Debate 280: Frank Turek vs Dennis Nørmark — Does God Exist? · 2014
entry.summary: Turek’s cumulative theistic case narrowly loses to Nørmark’s calibrated natural explanations, stronger concessions, and more consistent evidential burden.
